title: Silencing an Aquaporin Gene
topic: Cell structure and function · Membrane transport and gene expression

modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Biology Question 1 (Interpreting and Evaluating Experimental Results)

stimulus.content:
Part B, Table 1
Treatment | Relative AQP2 protein | Water permeability (µm/s)
No siRNA | 1.00 | 40 ± 4
Scrambled (control) siRNA | 0.98 | 39 ± 5
AQP2 siRNA | 0.12 | 10 ± 3

prompt: Aquaporin-2 (AQP2) is a channel protein in the plasma membrane of kidney collecting-duct cells. Researchers grew cultured collecting-duct cells and treated them in one of three ways: no treatment, a scrambled siRNA with no matching sequence in the cell, or an siRNA complementary to AQP2 mRNA. siRNA molecules bind complementary mRNA and cause it to be degraded. After 48 hours, the researchers measured the amount of AQP2 protein relative to untreated cells and the water permeability of the plasma membrane (Table 1). Values for permeability are mean ± 2 SE.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe how water moves across the plasma membrane through aquaporins.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes water moving passively (without ATP) through the aquaporin channel, down its water potential (or concentration) gradient, as facilitated diffusion.
commonErrors: says water moves from low to high water potential
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Water diffuses through the aquaporin channel from higher to lower water potential without using ATP.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Aquaporins use ATP to pump water into the cell.

parts.label: B
parts.text: (i) Identify the independent variable in the experiment. (ii) Justify the use of the scrambled siRNA treatment. (iii) State the null hypothesis for the comparison between the scrambled siRNA and AQP2 siRNA treatments.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the independent variable as the type of siRNA treatment.
commonErrors: identifies water permeability, the dependent variable
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The siRNA treatment the cells received.

rubricPoints.criterion: Justifies the scrambled siRNA as a control showing that any effect comes from silencing AQP2, not from the process of introducing an siRNA into the cells.
commonErrors: says it is a control without saying what it controls for
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: It shows that adding an siRNA by itself does not lower permeability, so any decrease must be due to silencing AQP2.

rubricPoints.criterion: States a null hypothesis of no difference: AQP2 siRNA does not change water permeability compared with scrambled siRNA.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: There is no difference in water permeability between cells treated with AQP2 siRNA and cells treated with scrambled siRNA.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: AQP2 siRNA will decrease water permeability.

figures.caption: Table 1
figures.alt: Table 1: Treatment No siRNA, Relative AQP2 protein 1.00, Water permeability (µm/s) 40 ± 4; Treatment Scrambled (control) siRNA, Relative AQP2 protein 0.98, Water permeability (µm/s) 39 ± 5; Treatment AQP2 siRNA, Relative AQP2 protein 0.12, Water permeability (µm/s) 10 ± 3

parts.label: C
parts.text: (i) Describe the effect of the AQP2 siRNA on water permeability compared with the scrambled siRNA, using data. (ii) Based on the data, determine whether the difference is statistically significant. (iii) The coding region of AQP2 mRNA, from the start codon through the stop codon, is 816 nucleotides long. Calculate the number of amino acids in the AQP2 polypeptide.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a decrease in permeability, from about 39 µm/s with scrambled siRNA to about 10 µm/s with AQP2 siRNA.
commonErrors: describes the protein data instead of permeability
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Permeability fell from 39 to 10 µm/s, about a 75% decrease.

rubricPoints.criterion: Concludes the difference is significant because the ±2 SE intervals (34–44 and 7–13 µm/s) do not overlap.
commonErrors: claims significance without referencing the intervals
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The intervals 34–44 and 7–13 do not overlap, so the difference is statistically significant.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: It is significant because 10 is much smaller than 39.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 271 amino acids (816 ÷ 3 = 272 codons, minus the stop codon).
commonErrors: counts the stop codon as an amino acid (272)
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: 816 / 3 = 272 codons; the stop codon codes for no amino acid, so 271.

parts.label: D
parts.text: A hormone causes collecting-duct cells to insert additional AQP2 proteins into their plasma membranes. (i) Predict how untreated cells exposed to the hormone would swell, compared with untreated cells without the hormone, after being moved to a hypotonic solution. (ii) Justify your prediction.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts that the hormone-treated cells swell faster.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: They swell faster.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: They swell at the same rate because the solution is the same.

rubricPoints.criterion: Justifies that more aquaporin channels in the membrane allow more water to enter per unit time down the water potential gradient.
commonErrors: says the hormone pumps water in
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: More channels give water more paths into the cell, so more water enters each second.

sampleResponse: A Water diffuses passively through the aquaporin channel, from higher to lower water potential, without ATP (facilitated diffusion). B (i) The siRNA treatment. (ii) It shows that introducing an siRNA by itself does not lower permeability, so a decrease with AQP2 siRNA is due to silencing AQP2. (iii) There is no difference in water permeability between cells treated with scrambled siRNA and with AQP2 siRNA. C (i) Permeability fell from 39 µm/s to 10 µm/s. (ii) Significant: the ±2 SE ranges 34–44 and 7–13 do not overlap. (iii) 816 / 3 = 272 codons, minus the stop codon = 271 amino acids. D (i) They swell faster. (ii) More AQP2 channels let more water enter per second down its water potential gradient.

title: Fish Alarm Substance and Its Receptor
topic: Cell communication · Signal transduction and behavior

modeledOn.type: Interpreting and Evaluating Experimental Results with Graphing
modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Biology Question 2 (Interpreting and Evaluating Experimental Results with Graphing)

stimulus.content:
Part B, Table 1
Fish | Added to tank | Time motionless (s)
Wild type | Water | 20 ± 6
Wild type | Skin extract | 150 ± 18
Receptor knockdown | Water | 22 ± 7
Receptor knockdown | Skin extract | 35 ± 10

prompt: When the skin of a small fish is damaged, it releases chemicals that cause nearby fish of the same species to stop moving (freeze). Researchers hypothesized that a receptor protein on olfactory neurons, receptor R, detects these chemicals. They used a morpholino to knock down receptor R in one group of fish. Fish were placed individually in tanks, either water or skin extract was added, and the time each fish spent motionless during a 300-second trial was recorded (Table 1). Values are mean ± 2 SE; n = 20 fish per group.

parts.label: A
parts.text: (i) Describe how binding of a chemical signal to a receptor on the plasma membrane of an olfactory neuron can lead to a response in the cell. (ii) Explain how the freezing response increases the fitness of fish that detect the alarm signal.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes ligand binding causing a change in the receptor’s shape that activates a signal transduction pathway (such as second messengers or opening ion channels) leading to a cellular response.
commonErrors: says the ligand enters the nucleus
no mention of a pathway or shape change
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Binding changes the receptor’s shape, which starts a cascade of second messengers that opens ion channels and triggers an action potential.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The chemical goes into the neuron.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that freezing makes a fish less likely to be detected by a nearby predator, increasing its survival and chance of reproducing.
commonErrors: says freezing helps the injured fish
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Motionless fish are harder for predators to spot, so they are more likely to survive and reproduce.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Using the data in Table 1, construct an appropriately labeled graph that represents the mean time motionless for each group, including the error bars.

rubricPoints.criterion: Constructs a bar graph (discrete groups) with correctly labeled axes, including units for time motionless, and a legend or labels distinguishing the four groups.
commonErrors: draws a line graph across categories
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: A bar graph with “Time motionless (s)” on the y-axis and the four genotype-treatment groups on the x-axis.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: A line connecting the four means.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses an appropriate linear scale and plots all four means correctly.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Bars at 20, 150, 22, and 35 s on a 0–200 s scale.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: A scale that jumps from 50 to 150.

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws error bars of ±2 SE correctly on all four bars.
commonErrors: draws error bars of only +2 SE
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Wild type with extract shows a bar from 132 to 168 s.

figures.caption: Table 1
figures.alt: Table 1: Fish Wild type, Added to tank Water, Time motionless (s) 20 ± 6; Fish Wild type, Added to tank Skin extract, Time motionless (s) 150 ± 18; Fish Receptor knockdown, Added to tank Water, Time motionless (s) 22 ± 7; Fish Receptor knockdown, Added to tank Skin extract, Time motionless (s) 35 ± 10

parts.label: C
parts.text: (i) Calculate the percent change in mean time motionless for wild-type fish exposed to skin extract compared with wild-type fish exposed to water. (ii) Based on the data, evaluate the researchers’ hypothesis that receptor R detects the alarm chemicals.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates a 650% increase ((150 − 20) / 20 × 100).
Supports the hypothesis, citing that knockdown fish barely respond to skin extract (35 s compared with 150 s for wild type) while responding normally to water (22 vs 20 s).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Supported: without receptor R, skin extract raises freezing only from 22 to 35 s, compared with 20 to 150 s in wild type.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Supported because the knockdown fish froze less.

parts.label: D
parts.text: (i) The researchers repeat the experiment with wild-type fish of a second species that lacks a gene for receptor R. Predict the time motionless when these fish are exposed to skin extract from the first species. (ii) Justify your prediction.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts little or no freezing, similar to the water control.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Close to the water control, about 20 s.

rubricPoints.criterion: Justifies that without receptor R the fish cannot detect the alarm chemicals, so the signal transduction pathway leading to freezing is not activated.
commonErrors: says the chemicals are toxic to the second species
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Without receptor R the chemical cannot bind, so the pathway that triggers freezing never starts.

sampleResponse: A (i) The chemical binds the receptor and changes its shape, which activates a signal transduction cascade (for example, a G protein and second messengers) that opens ion channels and produces an action potential. (ii) Freezing makes fish harder for nearby predators to detect, so they are more likely to survive and reproduce. B A bar graph with four bars (20, 150, 22, and 35 s), y-axis “Time motionless (s)” from 0 to 200, and ±2 SE error bars. C (i) (150 − 20) / 20 × 100 = 650% increase. (ii) Supported: knockdown fish respond to extract only slightly (35 s vs 22 s for water), while wild type increase from 20 to 150 s. D (i) About 20 s, like the water control. (ii) Without receptor R the alarm chemicals cannot bind, so the pathway that causes freezing is never activated.

title: Invasive Zebra Mussels and Native Mussels
prompt: Zebra mussels are invasive filter feeders that attach in large numbers to the shells of native mussels. Researchers placed native mussels in 12 identical tanks of lake water. In 6 tanks, the native mussels had zebra mussels attached; in the other 6 tanks they did not. After 8 weeks, the researchers measured the change in the native mussels’ tissue mass.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe one way that zebra mussels could reduce the growth of native mussels.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes competition for the same food (filtering phytoplankton from the water) or interference by covering the native mussel’s shell and openings.
commonErrors: says zebra mussels prey on native mussels
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Zebra mussels filter out the phytoplankton that native mussels also eat, leaving less food.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Zebra mussels eat the native mussels.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Identify the control group in this experiment.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the tanks with native mussels and no zebra mussels attached.
commonErrors: identifies the tanks with zebra mussels
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The six tanks in which native mussels had no zebra mussels.

parts.label: C
parts.text: State the null hypothesis for this experiment.

rubricPoints.criterion: States that attached zebra mussels have no effect on the change in native mussel tissue mass.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: There is no difference in tissue mass change between native mussels with and without zebra mussels.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Zebra mussels will reduce native mussel growth.

parts.label: D
parts.text: The researchers repeat the experiment with twice as much phytoplankton added to every tank. Predict how the difference in growth between the two groups would change, and justify your prediction.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts the difference decreases, justified by reduced competition for food when food is more plentiful.
commonErrors: predicts a larger difference without reasoning
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The difference shrinks, because with more food the zebra mussels take less of what the native mussels need.

sampleResponse: A Zebra mussels filter the same phytoplankton native mussels eat, reducing their food. B The six tanks with native mussels and no attached zebra mussels. C There is no difference in tissue mass change between native mussels with and without attached zebra mussels. D The difference decreases; with abundant phytoplankton, competition for food is reduced, so the zebra mussels limit native growth less.

title: Pupfish in Isolated Springs
prompt: About 10,000 years ago, a large lake in a desert region dried up, leaving several small, separate springs. Each spring now holds a small population of pupfish descended from the original lake population. The springs differ in temperature and salinity, and fish from different springs now differ in body shape and coloration.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify the type of reproductive isolation that first separated the pupfish populations.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies geographic isolation (allopatric separation).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Geographic isolation: the springs are physically separated.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Explain why genetic drift is likely to have had a larger effect on allele frequencies in the spring populations than in the original lake population.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that the spring populations are small, so random chance events change allele frequencies more (and can fix or eliminate alleles).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: In small populations, chance differences in which fish reproduce shift allele frequencies a lot.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The fish adapted to the springs.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Explain how natural selection could produce differences in body shape between populations in springs of different temperature.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that heritable variations in body shape that improve survival and reproduction in a given spring’s conditions become more common there over generations.
commonErrors: says fish change shape because they need to
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Fish with a body shape suited to their spring’s temperature survive and reproduce more, so that heritable shape increases in frequency.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The fish changed shape to survive the heat.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Fish from two springs are brought together in a lab, and their hybrid offspring are much less likely to survive than either parent type. Predict how selection would affect mate preference if the two populations continued to live together, and justify your prediction.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts that selection favors fish that mate only with their own population (prezygotic barriers strengthen, reinforcement), because those fish do not waste reproduction on low-fitness hybrids.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Fish that prefer mates from their own spring will leave more surviving offspring, so the preference spreads.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: They will interbreed and become one species.

sampleResponse: A Geographic isolation. B The spring populations are small, so random variation in which individuals reproduce shifts allele frequencies much more than in a large population. C In each spring, heritable body shapes that improve survival and reproduction under that spring’s temperature become more common over generations. D Selection favors fish that mate only with their own population, because they avoid producing hybrids that rarely survive; prezygotic isolation strengthens (reinforcement).

title: Feedback Inhibition in an Energy Pathway

modeledOn.type: Analysis of a Model or Visual Representation
modeledOn.label: 2025 AP Biology Question 5 (Analysis of a Model or Visual Representation)

stimulus.content: Figure 1: A pathway: sugar S is converted by enzyme 1 to intermediate I1, by enzyme 2 to I2, and by enzyme 3 to products including ATP. A dashed arrow from ATP returns to enzyme 1 with a minus sign, showing inhibition

prompt: Figure 1 is a model of a metabolic pathway in which three enzymes convert a sugar, S, into intermediates and eventually produce ATP. ATP binds to an allosteric site on enzyme 1 and reduces its activity.

figures.alt: A pathway: sugar S is converted by enzyme 1 to intermediate I1, by enzyme 2 to I2, and by enzyme 3 to products including ATP. A dashed arrow from ATP returns to enzyme 1 with a minus sign, showing inhibition
figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe how binding of ATP to the allosteric site reduces the activity of enzyme 1.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes ATP binding at a site other than the active site and changing the enzyme’s shape so the active site binds substrate less effectively.
commonErrors: says ATP binds the active site (competitive inhibition)
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: ATP binds away from the active site and changes enzyme 1’s shape, so S fits the active site less well.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Explain how this regulation helps the cell maintain a stable ATP supply.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains negative feedback: when ATP is high the pathway slows, conserving S; when ATP falls, inhibition is released and the pathway speeds up.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: High ATP shuts the pathway down; as ATP is used up, enzyme 1 becomes active again and ATP production resumes.

parts.label: C
parts.text: A mutation changes the allosteric site of enzyme 1 so that ATP can no longer bind. Predict the effect of the mutation on the amount of S used by the cell when its energy demand is low.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts that the cell uses more S (the pathway keeps running) when energy demand is low.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: More S is used, because the pathway no longer slows down when ATP is plentiful.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Justify why enzyme 1, rather than enzyme 3, is the regulated step in this pathway.

rubricPoints.criterion: Justifies that regulating the first step prevents the cell from spending S and producing intermediates (I₁, I₂) that it does not need.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Stopping the first step avoids wasting S and building up unused intermediates.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Enzyme 1 is the most important enzyme.

sampleResponse: A ATP binds a site away from the active site and changes enzyme 1’s shape, so the active site binds S less effectively. B This is negative feedback: when ATP is plentiful the pathway slows, and when ATP is used up the inhibition is released and ATP production speeds up again. C The cell uses more S, because the pathway keeps running even when ATP is high. D Regulating the first step keeps the cell from spending S and accumulating intermediates it does not need.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Calculate the frequency of the HbS allele in the population.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates q = 0.21 (0.02 + ½ × 0.38).

parts.label: B
parts.text: Calculate the expected frequency of heterozygotes if the population were in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates 2pq ≈ 0.33 (2 × 0.79 × 0.21), or a value consistent with part A.
commonErrors: uses pq without the factor of 2

parts.label: C
parts.text: The observed frequency of heterozygotes differs from the expected frequency. Explain the difference.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that there are more heterozygotes than expected because heterozygotes survive malaria better (and HbS homozygotes have reduced survival), so the genotypes are not equally fit.
commonErrors: attributes the difference only to random mating
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Observed 0.38 exceeds the expected 0.33 because heterozygotes are more likely to survive malaria to adulthood.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Predict how the frequency of the HbS allele would change over many generations if malaria were eliminated from the region. Justify your prediction.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts the HbS frequency decreases, because heterozygotes no longer have an advantage while HbS homozygotes still have lower fitness.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: It decreases: without malaria, carrying HbS no longer helps, but HbS/HbS individuals still have sickle cell disease.

sampleResponse: A q = 0.02 + ½(0.38) = 0.21. B 2pq = 2(0.79)(0.21) ≈ 0.33. C There are more heterozygotes than expected (0.38 vs 0.33) because heterozygotes are more resistant to malaria and more of them survive to adulthood, while HbS/HbS individuals have reduced survival. D It decreases over generations; without malaria, heterozygotes have no advantage, but selection against HbS/HbS individuals continues.

figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe how increasing root hair length could help a plant growing in low-phosphate soil.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes that longer root hairs increase the root’s surface area (and soil volume reached), increasing the rate of phosphate absorption.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Longer root hairs give more surface area in contact with soil, so the plant can absorb more phosphate.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Root hairs make the plant taller.

parts.label: B
parts.text: (i) Identify the dependent variable. (ii) Identify the group that serves as the control for the effect of RHP on wild-type plants. (iii) Justify the researchers’ decision to include rk mutant plants.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies mean root hair length as the dependent variable.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Mean root hair length.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies wild-type plants grown without RHP.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Wild-type plants with no added RHP.

rubricPoints.criterion: Justifies that comparing mutants with wild type tests whether the RHP effect requires the RK receptor.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: If RHP has no effect on plants that lack RK, then RK is needed for the RHP response.

parts.label: C
parts.text: (i) Calculate the percent increase in mean root hair length when RHP is added to wild-type plants. (ii) Using the error bars, determine whether RHP had a statistically significant effect on rk mutant plants. (iii) Based on the data, make a claim about the role of RK in the response to RHP.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates about a 113% increase ((0.85 − 0.40) / 0.40 × 100).
Determines the effect on rk mutants is not significant because the error bars overlap (0.33–0.43 and 0.36–0.46 mm).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Not significant: the ±2 SE ranges overlap.

rubricPoints.criterion: Claims RK is required for (is the receptor for) the RHP response, because RHP lengthens root hairs only in plants with functional RK.
commonErrors: claims RK inhibits root hair growth
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: RK is required for the response to RHP: RHP doubles root hair length in wild type but has no effect without RK.

parts.label: D
parts.text: A different mutation produces an RK protein that is always active, even without RHP. (i) Predict the root hair length of these mutants grown without RHP, compared with wild-type plants without RHP. (ii) Justify your prediction.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts longer root hairs than wild type without RHP (similar to wild type with RHP).
commonErrors: predicts the same as wild type
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Longer, about the length of wild type with RHP.

rubricPoints.criterion: Justifies that the always-active receptor triggers the signaling pathway for root hair elongation without needing the peptide signal.
commonErrors: says the plant makes more RHP
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: An always-active RK starts the elongation pathway on its own, so RHP binding is not needed.

sampleResponse: A Longer root hairs increase the surface area in contact with soil, so the plant absorbs more of the scarce phosphate. B (i) Mean root hair length. (ii) Wild-type plants without RHP. (iii) Mutants test whether the RHP effect requires RK; if RHP does not work without RK, RK is needed for the response. C (i) (0.85 − 0.40) / 0.40 × 100 ≈ 113%. (ii) Not significant: the ±2 SE ranges (0.33–0.43 and 0.36–0.46) overlap. (iii) RK is required for the RHP response, because RHP more than doubles root hair length only in plants with RK. D (i) Longer than wild type without RHP, close to wild type with RHP. (ii) An always-active RK triggers the elongation pathway without the peptide.

title: One Transcription Factor, Two Target Genes
topic: Gene expression and regulation · Transcription factors

modeledOn.type: Interpreting and Evaluating Experimental Results with Graphing
modeledOn.label: 2026 AP Biology Question 2 (Interpreting and Evaluating Experimental Results with Graphing)

stimulus.content:
Part B, Table 1
Genotype | Relative J mRNA | Relative K mRNA
Wild type | 1.0 ± 0.1 | 1.0 ± 0.1
tf knockout | 0.2 ± 0.05 | 2.4 ± 0.3
TF overexpression | 3.1 ± 0.3 | 0.4 ± 0.08

prompt: Researchers studied a transcription factor, TF, in a species of yeast. They measured the amount of mRNA from two genes, J and K, in wild-type cells, cells with the TF gene knocked out (tf knockout), and cells that overexpress TF. mRNA amounts are given relative to wild type (Table 1) as mean ± 2 SE.

parts.label: A
parts.text: (i) Describe how a transcription factor can regulate the expression of a gene. (ii) Explain why the researchers measured mRNA rather than protein to study the effect of TF on transcription.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a transcription factor binding a regulatory DNA sequence (promoter or enhancer) and increasing or decreasing RNA polymerase binding or transcription initiation.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: TF binds a regulatory sequence near the gene and helps or blocks RNA polymerase from starting transcription.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: TF binds the mRNA and destroys it.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that mRNA is the direct product of transcription, while protein levels also depend on translation and protein degradation.
commonErrors: says mRNA is easier to see
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: mRNA directly reflects transcription; protein amounts can also change through translation or degradation.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: Protein is too small to measure.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Using the data in Table 1, construct an appropriately labeled graph that represents the relative mRNA of genes J and K for each genotype, including error bars.

rubricPoints.criterion: Constructs a grouped bar graph with labeled axes (relative mRNA amount; genotype) and a key distinguishing genes J and K.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Paired bars for J and K above each genotype, with a key.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: A line through the three genotypes.

rubricPoints.criterion: Uses an appropriate linear scale and plots all six means correctly.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Bars at 1.0, 0.2, 3.1 for J and 1.0, 2.4, 0.4 for K on a 0–3.5 scale.

rubricPoints.criterion: Draws ±2 SE error bars correctly on all six bars.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: TF overexpression J bar has an error bar from 2.8 to 3.4.

figures.caption: Table 1
figures.alt: Table 1: Genotype Wild type, Relative J mRNA 1.0 ± 0.1, Relative K mRNA 1.0 ± 0.1; Genotype tf knockout, Relative J mRNA 0.2 ± 0.05, Relative K mRNA 2.4 ± 0.3; Genotype TF overexpression, Relative J mRNA 3.1 ± 0.3, Relative K mRNA 0.4 ± 0.08

parts.label: C
parts.text: (i) Calculate the percent change in K mRNA in tf knockout cells compared with wild type. (ii) Based on the data, make a claim about how TF affects the transcription of genes J and K.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates a 140% increase ((2.4 − 1.0) / 1.0 × 100).
Claims TF activates J and represses K, supported by J falling and K rising without TF, and the opposite with extra TF.
commonErrors: claims TF affects both genes the same way
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: TF activates J and represses K: removing TF lowers J and raises K, and overexpressing TF does the reverse.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: TF controls genes J and K.

parts.label: D
parts.text: (i) Predict the amount of K mRNA in otherwise wild-type cells with a mutation that prevents TF from binding the regulatory sequence of gene K. (ii) Justify your prediction.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts K mRNA increases above wild type (similar to the knockout, about 2.4).
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: K mRNA rises to about the knockout level.

rubricPoints.criterion: Justifies that TF can no longer repress K, while J is still regulated normally because its binding site is intact.
commonErrors: says TF is no longer made
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: TF is still made and still activates J, but it cannot bind K’s regulatory sequence, so K is no longer repressed.

sampleResponse: A (i) A transcription factor binds a regulatory DNA sequence such as a promoter or enhancer and increases or decreases RNA polymerase binding, changing how often the gene is transcribed. (ii) mRNA is the direct product of transcription; protein levels also depend on translation and degradation. B A grouped bar graph: for each genotype a J bar and a K bar (1.0/1.0, 0.2/2.4, 3.1/0.4) with ±2 SE error bars, a y-axis “Relative mRNA amount,” and a key. C (i) (2.4 − 1.0) / 1.0 × 100 = 140% increase. (ii) TF activates J and represses K. D (i) K mRNA increases to about the knockout level. (ii) TF can no longer bind K’s regulatory sequence, so it cannot repress K.

title: Rotenone and Yeast Respiration
prompt: Rotenone is a compound that blocks the transfer of electrons from NADH to the first protein complex of the electron transport chain. Rotenone is dissolved in ethanol before use. Researchers grew yeast in a glucose solution and added either rotenone dissolved in ethanol or no treatment, then measured the rate of oxygen consumption by the yeast.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify the independent variable in the experiment.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies the presence or absence of rotenone.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Whether rotenone was added.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Identify an additional control group the researchers should include, and justify its use.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies yeast given ethanol alone (the solvent without rotenone), justified as showing that any effect is caused by rotenone and not the ethanol.
commonErrors: suggests a group with no yeast without justification
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Yeast given the same amount of ethanol without rotenone, to show the ethanol itself does not change oxygen use.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Predict how rotenone will affect the rate of oxygen consumption by the yeast.

rubricPoints.criterion: Predicts that oxygen consumption decreases.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: It decreases.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: It increases because the yeast need more energy.

parts.label: D
parts.text: Justify your prediction in part C.

rubricPoints.criterion: Justifies that with electrons blocked from entering the chain, fewer electrons reach oxygen, the final electron acceptor, so less oxygen is reduced to water.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Electrons from NADH cannot enter the chain, so fewer electrons reach O₂ at the end and less O₂ is used to form water.

sampleResponse: A The presence or absence of rotenone. B Yeast given the same volume of ethanol without rotenone; this shows that any change is caused by rotenone and not by the ethanol solvent. C Oxygen consumption decreases. D Rotenone stops electrons from NADH entering the electron transport chain, so fewer electrons are passed to oxygen, the final electron acceptor, and less oxygen is reduced to water.

title: Nondisjunction in Meiosis II
prompt: In a species with a diploid number of 2n = 4, a germ cell undergoes meiosis. Meiosis I proceeds normally. In meiosis II, the sister chromatids of one chromosome fail to separate in one of the two cells; the other cell divides normally.

parts.label: A
parts.text: Describe what normally happens to sister chromatids during anaphase II.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes the sister chromatids separating and moving to opposite poles of the cell.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The sister chromatids of each chromosome separate and are pulled to opposite poles.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Identify the number of chromosomes in each of the four gametes produced.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies 3, 1, 2, and 2 chromosomes.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: One gamete has 3, one has 1, and two have 2.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Explain the result if the gamete with the extra chromosome is fertilized by a normal gamete.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that the zygote has 5 chromosomes (2n + 1), three copies of one chromosome (trisomy), which can disrupt development through altered gene dosage.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The zygote has 5 chromosomes, with three copies of one chromosome (trisomy).

parts.label: D
parts.text: Explain why nondisjunction during meiosis I would produce a different set of gametes than nondisjunction during meiosis II.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that in meiosis I a homologous pair fails to separate, so both daughter cells and all four gametes are abnormal (two n + 1 and two n − 1), whereas in meiosis II only the gametes from one cell are affected.
commonErrors: states the outcomes are the same
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: If homologs fail to separate in meiosis I, both cells are abnormal and all four gametes have the wrong number; in meiosis II only two gametes are affected.

sampleResponse: A The sister chromatids of each chromosome separate and move to opposite poles. B 3, 1, 2, and 2 chromosomes. C The zygote has 5 chromosomes (2n + 1), with three copies of one chromosome (trisomy). D In meiosis I a homologous pair fails to separate, so both daughter cells are abnormal and all four gametes have the wrong number (3, 3, 1, 1); in meiosis II only the two gametes from the affected cell are abnormal.

commonErrors: predicts it returns to the original mean immediately

rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The same as before the drought.

figures.caption: Figure 1

parts.label: A
parts.text: Identify the median number of tadpoles per sample in Watershed 2.

rubricPoints.criterion: Identifies a median of 30 tadpoles per sample.
commonErrors: reports the mean or a quartile
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: 30 tadpoles per sample.

parts.label: B
parts.text: Describe the relationship between pesticide level and the number of tadpoles per sample.

rubricPoints.criterion: Describes a negative relationship: as pesticide level increases, the number of tadpoles per sample decreases.
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: Higher pesticide levels go with fewer tadpoles per sample.

parts.label: C
parts.text: Calculate the percent decrease in the median number of tadpoles per sample from Watershed 1 to Watershed 3.

rubricPoints.criterion: Calculates about a 64% decrease ((42 − 15) / 42 × 100).

parts.label: D
parts.text: A student claims these data show that the pesticide causes the decline in tadpoles. Evaluate the claim.

rubricPoints.criterion: Explains that the data are observational (a correlation), so other differences between watersheds could cause the decline; a controlled experiment that varies only pesticide would be needed to show causation.
commonErrors: accepts the claim because the trend is clear
rubricPoints.exampleEarning: The claim is not fully supported: the watersheds may differ in other ways, such as habitat or predators, so a controlled experiment is needed.
rubricPoints.exampleFailing: The claim is correct because Watershed 3 has the fewest tadpoles.

sampleResponse: A 30 tadpoles per sample. B As pesticide level increases, the number of tadpoles per sample decreases. C (42 − 15) / 42 × 100 ≈ 64% decrease. D Not fully supported: the study is observational, so other differences between watersheds (habitat, predators, temperature) could explain the decline. A controlled experiment that varies only pesticide concentration would be needed to show causation.
